title: What are computer-use agents?
description: Understand the observe–plan–act loop, how GUI agents differ from browser automation, and which research resources help you get started.
body:
COMPUTER-USE AGENT GUIDE

What are computer-use agents?

A computer-use agent is an AI system that observes a software interface, decides what action to take, executes it, and checks the resulting state to work toward a user’s goal. The interface may be a browser, desktop application, or mobile device.

Some systems act mainly through screenshots, clicks, and keystrokes. Others combine graphical interaction with code and tool calls. These are two execution designs, and each is compared on its own terms. See the primary descriptions of UI-TARS and OpenGCUA.

How does a computer-use agent work?

  1. Observe: obtain screenshots, page structure, accessibility information, or other exposed state.
  2. Plan and ground: decide a useful next step and identify the interface element or tool that can perform it.
  3. Act: click, type, scroll, invoke a tool, or execute code within the system’s permitted interface.
  4. Check: inspect the new state, determine progress, and retry, replan, stop, or ask for help.

This is a practical decomposition rather than a single mandated architecture. Agent S is one example that combines planning with retrieved experience and a computer interaction interface.

Are GUI grounding and task completion the same?

No. Grounding asks whether a model can locate the correct target on a screen. Task completion additionally involves choosing the right actions, handling transitions, tracking progress, and verifying the final result. Finishing a long workflow takes more than a strong grounding score.

ScreenSpot-Pro evaluates grounding in professional interfaces, while OSWorld evaluates tasks in real computer environments. Use the benchmark appropriate to the capability you want to measure.

Which resources should I start with?

  • For desktop evaluation: benchmarks and the OSWorld paper.
  • For model behavior and perception: GUI model families and checkpoints.
  • For training: training data and supervision types.
  • For deployment: frameworks and execution environments.
  • For the literature: reviewed papers and surveys.

How should I interpret this catalog?

A repository, a paper, a dataset, and a model checkpoint can describe related parts of one project. The editorial policy explains how records are reviewed.

Editorial update: 2026-10-16. This guide synthesizes the linked primary research.

title: How to choose a GUI-agent benchmark
description: Compare desktop task execution, browser workflows, mobile environments, and GUI grounding, and preserve the evaluation conditions needed for meaningful comparisons.
body:
EVALUATION GUIDE

How to choose a GUI-agent benchmark

Choose a benchmark by the capability and environment you need to measure. Screenshot target localization, live website navigation, Android workflows, and cross-application desktop tasks answer different questions.

BenchmarkEnvironmentPrimary focus
OSWorldReal desktop environmentsTask outcomes checked through execution and application/system state.
WebArenaReproducible websitesFunctional completion of web tasks.
AndroidWorldAndroid applicationsParameterized interactive tasks with initialization and success checks.
ScreenSpot-ProProfessional interface screenshotsPrecise localization of requested GUI targets.

Compare source-reviewed benchmark protocols, task populations, and interfaces.

Which benchmark is best?

There is no single answer without a deployment target. For a desktop assistant, start with desktop task execution. For a browser agent, use web tasks and the relevant site conditions. For mobile control, test the mobile environment. For a grounding model, isolate target localization before interpreting end-to-end task outcomes. This recommendation follows from the different tasks defined by the linked benchmark papers.

What must be recorded with a score?

  • The benchmark version or commit and task split.
  • The exact model checkpoint, agent harness, tools, and observation interface.
  • The action or step budget and any retries or multiple attempts.
  • The evaluator, success criterion, and aggregation method.
  • The environment setup, run date, and whether sites or apps changed.
  • Whether the result was reproduced independently or reported by the publisher.

Without these details, apparently similar percentages may refer to different experiments. Rank static grounding accuracy and completed-task rate separately.

How do I check reproducibility?

Follow the benchmark’s current official setup and evaluation instructions. Compare them with the version used in the paper. The current OSWorld repository, WebArena repository, and AndroidWorld repository are starting points. A reproduction succeeds when your run matches the reported setup and results.

Where can I find more benchmarks?

Browse the reviewed benchmark directory or use the interactive benchmark filter. Each resource exposes its primary evidence and any recorded specifications.

Editorial update: 2026-10-16.

title: Where to find training data for GUI agents
description: Distinguish grounding examples, interaction trajectories, screen understanding data, and benchmark tasks, with primary dataset sources and separate licensing checks.
body:
TRAINING DATA GUIDE

Where to find training data for GUI agents

Start with the supervision your model needs: screen understanding, element grounding, individual actions, or complete interaction trajectories. Then match the platform, annotation format, split, and license before downloading.

Which data types are useful?

  • Screen understanding: screenshots paired with descriptions, questions, or structural annotations.
  • Grounding: an instruction and screen paired with a target element or location.
  • Action prediction: observations and instructions paired with the next action.
  • Trajectories: sequences of observations and actions that show how a task unfolds.

These supervision types support different objectives. Task coverage is measured by the demonstrations a dataset contains.

What are concrete starting points?

ResourceWhat to inspect
Android in the WildAndroid task demonstrations with screens, instructions, and actions; distinguish episodes from action examples.
AndroidControlHigh-level task goals, step instructions, screenshots, accessibility trees, and action annotations.
AgentNetComputer-use demonstrations associated with the OpenCUA research stack.
OS-Atlas dataGUI grounding data and the publisher’s access and licensing declaration.
Mind2WebWeb-task demonstrations and generalization splits across sites and domains.

Compare source-reviewed dataset formats, counting units, and splits.

Can I use benchmark examples for training?

Check the intended split and evaluation protocol first. Training on examples used to measure generalization can invalidate the comparison you wanted to make. Preserve the split definitions and document any overlap or filtering decisions rather than treating every downloadable task as training data.

Does an open code repository imply open training data?

No. Code, datasets, and model weights may be distributed under different licenses. Check the current dataset card, original collection terms, access restrictions, and any upstream components. AwesomeCUA records these declarations separately and leaves unknown values empty. Rights to each asset come from its own license and terms.

How do I compare dataset scale?

Keep units explicit: tasks, episodes, actions, screenshots, instructions, and UI elements are different quantities. A hosting platform’s size category may count packaged files rather than semantic examples. Compare the quantity that matches the intended training objective.

Continue with the reviewed dataset directory or searchable dataset catalog. Use our metadata export to inspect sources and licenses programmatically; it contains the resource records.
